name: WebGPU features and limits
plain: Reads which optional WebGPU features and numeric limits the GPU supports.
meaning: About 30 limits and 15 optional features (for example shader-f16, timestamp-query) form a fine-grained hardware and driver signature, usable for model-size gating and for fingerprinting.

data.metric: About 30 integer limits and up to 20 feature flags

limits.headline: Can list which optional graphics features and limits your device supports
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when the page uses WebGPU
can: List about 30 hardware limits and 15 optional features
Build a fine hardware and driver profile
Decide which size of AI model your device can run
Add the profile to a device ID
cannot: Work in browsers without WebGPU support

story.what_it_is: A script reads which optional WebGPU features and number limits your graphics chip supports.

marketing.name: WebGPU
marketing.pitch: Chrome describes WebGPU as giving the web modern graphics and computing power similar to native apps.

marketing.name: GPUSupportedLimits
marketing.pitch: Describes the numbers that tell a page how large and complex the graphics jobs can be.

story.for_you: You never see it. The page asks how big and complex a job your graphics chip can handle, then picks settings for you. Your answers also add to a unique profile of your device.
story.for_makers: Game, 3D and on device AI apps read these limits to decide what to run. The numbers also split devices by chip and driver, so browsers round or hide some values.

use_cases.example: A browser game checks the largest texture and buffer sizes, then picks scene detail that fits your chip.
A web 3D tool checks features before it turns on advanced shadow and light effects.
A web app that runs an AI chat model locally checks memory limits first so it does not crash.
A browser video tool decides how many effects it can apply at once.
A fraud tool compares limits with what the claimed device should show, and finds mismatches.
A tracker uses the exact limits as extra bits for a device ID.
A developer uses the numbers to know why a scene runs well on one laptop and badly on another.

risks: New and not yet well defended

technical_bounds: Many limits cluster into a few tiers, lowering uniqueness
